Consult Summary:
- 35-year-old male lawyer with several weeks–months of new intermittent frontal headaches plus systemic adrenergic-type symptoms (palpitations, feeling hot/short of breath, bilateral hand tingling), unintentional 5 lb weight loss, reduced appetite and decreased libido beginning around a job change; plan for in-person cardiorespiratory exam and thyroid blood tests.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Intermittent severe frontal headaches affecting work.
  - Episodic palpitations, sensation of rapid heartbeat (~once/day, maybe more).
  - Episodic feeling hot / shortness of breath while sitting at desk.
  - Bilateral hand tingling described as “quick picking,” often when entering an elevator or at work.
  - Decreased appetite, unintentional ~5 lb weight loss.
  - Decreased libido.
- Timeline / progression:
  - Symptoms began around the time of a job change (several weeks–months).
  - Symptoms are intermittent and episodic, usually occurring at work (meetings or at computer).
  - No prior history of similar headaches before this job change.
- Exacerbating / relieving factors:
  - Mostly provoked by work situations (meetings, computer work); no clear relieving factors reported.
- Associated symptoms / review of systems:
  - Mild nausea with headaches.
  - Shortness of breath during episodes while at rest; not reported with exercise.
  - No leg paresthesias.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - Denies chest pain, syncope, illicit drug use (including cocaine, marijuana), and smoking.
  - No prior frequent headaches before current illness.
  - No documented visual changes, focal neurological deficits, or fevers.

Past Medical History:
- History of “hyperthyroidism” as reported by patient.
  - Patient reports taking thyroxine. (Conflict noted: hyperthyroidism would usually not be treated with thyroxine; see Quality checks.)
- No other medical problems documented.

Medications:
- Thyroxine — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- No other medications documented.

Allergies:
- None reported.

Social History:
- Occupation: Lawyer, works in London; high occupational stress (patient rates 7–8/10).
- Alcohol: Drinks approximately once per week, a couple of glasses of wine.
- Tobacco: Denies current smoking.
- Recreational drugs: Denies use.
- No other social/financial issues documented.

Family History:
- Not documented in the transcript.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings: Not recorded; clinician recommended an in-person exam of heart and lungs.

Investigations:
- Planned: in-person cardiovascular and respiratory examination.
- Planned: blood tests for thyroid function (clinician: “do some blood tests, for your thyroxine”) — specific tests not listed in transcript.
- No ECG, imaging, or lab results reported at time of consult.

Assessment & Plan:

Overall Impression:
- Working impression: Symptoms most consistent with thyroid dysfunction (possible thyrotoxicosis/overreplacement) and/or work-related anxiety/panic contributing to episodic palpitations, shortness of breath, and paresthesias. Headaches likely multifactorial with a contribution from workplace/ergonomic factors. Further in-person assessment and thyroid testing are required.

DDx Integration (brief):
- Thyrotoxicosis (iatrogenic overreplacement or uncontrolled hyperthyroidism)
  - Supporting: Patient-reported thyroid disease, currently taking thyroxine; classic symptoms present — palpitations, heat intolerance/feeling hot, weight loss, decreased libido.
  - Opposing: Patient described “hyperthyroidism” yet reports taking thyroxine (possible history/terminology inconsistency); no laboratory confirmation yet.
  - (DDx and transcript both highlight thyroid dysfunction as high likelihood; conflict between reported diagnosis and medication use — see Quality checks.)
- Anxiety disorder / Panic attacks (work-related)
  - Supporting: Symptoms occur mostly at work/meetings; high occupational stress (7–8/10); episodic palpitations, shortness of breath, tingling and nausea fit anxiety/panic presentations.
  - Opposing: Thyroid dysfunction or arrhythmia could explain many symptoms and should be excluded.
- Tension-type / cervicogenic headache with ergonomic strain (and possible median nerve irritation / carpal tunnel)
  - Supporting: Headaches are frontal, occur with computer/meeting work; bilateral hand tingling in a computer worker.
  - Opposing: Does not explain systemic adrenergic features (palpitations, weight loss, heat intolerance).

Issue 1: Possible thyroid dysfunction / thyrotoxicosis
- Summary:
  - Patient reports history of thyroid disease and current thyroxine use with multiple symptoms suggestive of thyrotoxicosis (palpitations, heat intolerance, weight loss, reduced libido).
  - Transcript and DDx note inconsistency between reported “hyperthyroidism” and current thyroxine therapy (potential overreplacement or misstatement).
- Plan:
  - Arrange in-person clinic visit for focused exam (cardiac, respiratory, general).
  - Order thyroid function tests (to evaluate thyroxine/TSH and confirm thyroid status) — clinician indicated thyroid blood tests.
  - Review thyroxine medication (dose/route/frequency) and adherence; verify prescription details and consider endocrine input if abnormal results.
  - Do not start or change thyroid-directed medication remotely; clinician explicitly deferred medication changes until in-person assessment.
  - Advise patient to book clinic appointment via app (as discussed).

Issue 2: Anxiety / work-related panic symptoms
- Summary:
  - Symptoms are temporally related to work/meetings, high reported stress, and episodic autonomic symptoms consistent with anxiety/panic contributing to presentation.
- Plan:
  - Assess for anxiety/panic disorder during in-person visit (history and mental health screen).
  - Provide initial supportive advice and discuss workplace stressors; consider referral to primary care mental health or occupational health if indicated (to be decided after clinic assessment).
  - Monitor symptom pattern and severity; consider further interventions if clinically appropriate after assessment.

Issue 3: Headache and bilateral hand tingling (ergonomic / cervicogenic / peripheral nerve)
- Summary:
  - Frontal headaches occurring during prolonged computer/meeting work, started after job change; bilateral hand tingling related to work/posture.
- Plan:
  - Perform focused neurological and musculoskeletal exam in clinic (neck, upper limb, peripheral nerve testing).
  - Provide ergonomic advice and consider workplace adjustments; if symptoms persist or focal exam signs present, consider targeted investigation/referral (to be determined after in-person exam).

General plan items:
- Patient to be seen in clinic for physical examination and thyroid blood tests; clinician will communicate findings to the seeing clinician to avoid repeating history.
- No medications to be initiated or altered before in-person assessment.
- If palpitations or shortness of breath become severe, or if new chest pain, syncope, or marked functional decline occur, seek urgent/emergency care (patient advised to return promptly if symptoms worsen).

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Vital signs and physical examination findings are not recorded (not performed during this remote consult).
  - Thyroxine dose/route/frequency not documented — medication details need confirmation.
  - Family history not documented.
  - No ECG or ambulatory cardiac monitoring documented — may be appropriate if palpitations persist (DDx suggested arrhythmia; to be considered after clinic exam).
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - Patient reports diagnosis of “hyperthyroidism” yet also reports taking thyroxine; DDx flagged possible iatrogenic overreplacement and noted this inconsistency. Conflict noted.
- Transcript quality:
  - Audio transcript overall adequate; some short pauses and conversational fragments but key clinical details are clearly documented.
